bib.title: Machine Learning Engineering in Action, chapter 16: Production infrastructure

question: How should a team manage model artifacts, features and prediction serving so that production ML is reproducible, consistent and no more complex or costly than its SLA, volume and recency needs require?
contributions: Passive retraining with an MLflow model registry for provenance and rollback
Feature stores for training/serving consistency, reuse and cross-team access (Databricks example)
A serving-architecture decision framework from SLA, cost, recency and volume: batch, microservice, microbatch streaming, elastic REST, edge

results.claim: In a hotel-deal recommender, precalculated batch predictions reached fewer than 5% of sessions, so the A/B test showed no booking-rate difference from control.
results.setup: Illustrative scenario (hotel price optimizer, NoSQL-backed REST API serving precalculated lists), not a measured study
results.quote: fewer than 5% of sessions utilized the predictions, forcing the remaining 95% of page displays to show the fallback logic

results.claim: Example active-retraining trigger: retrain when the 48-hour windowed forecast accuracy drops below 70%.
results.setup: Hypothetical next-hour weather prediction with hour-lagged ground truth

results.claim: Batch serving suits freshness of hours to weeks; real-time REST is needed when predictions are used immediately (Fig 16.10 thresholds: high >100K/hour, moderate 1K-100K/hour, low 1-100/hour).
A lightweight Flask model deployment can support up to a few dozen requests per second, and is inappropriate for low-latency, high-volume or customer-facing use.
results.setup: Internal ad hoc microservice, author's experience
results.quote: Capable of supporting up to a few dozen requests per second

results.claim: Microbatch streaming suits very high volume with moderate SLA of 0.5-5 s, or high SLA (hours/days) with burst ingestion.

Illustrative gated vs ungated delivery: ungated weekly volumes of 27.6, 11.8, 198.3, 8 and 832.9 GB gave delivery times from 6:01 a.m. to 4:32 p.m. (worst week 7 hr 18 min of prediction), while gating egress at 9:00 a.m. gives consistent delivery.

results.claim: Low-volume REST services are tens to thousands of requests per minute and need only simple deployment and monitoring.
results.quote: (tens to thousands of requests per minute)

limits: Opinion and experience of one practitioner; no measured experiments, all numbers are illustrations.

Code is Databricks/Spark/MLflow-specific; the book itself warns feature store APIs may change significantly. MLflow stage-based registry (Production/Archived stages) has since been superseded by aliases in newer MLflow (not stated in chapter).
Active retraining is only described, no reference architecture given.
Traffic tiers and latency figures (5 ms, 200 ms, 0.5-5 s SLA) are heuristics without sources.
practices: Use a model registry for scheduled (passive) retraining: log each retraining run, promote only if it beats production on the same holdout, archive the old version (16.1.1, p.475).
Keep a registry status table (model_name, production_version, updated, training_time) in Delta for historical provenance (16.1.2, p.476-478).
Prefer passive retraining over active unless passive stops working; active needs monitoring, ground-truth merging and thresholds and is expensive (p.481).
Use a feature store so feature logic is defined once, shared by training and serving, and accessible to other teams (16.2, p.483-485).
Register the model through the feature store API so feature engineering is bundled with the model artifact and batch scoring needs only score_batch (Listing 16.8-16.9, p.488-489).
Evaluate feature stores on: sync to online serving, accessibility, batch and streaming ingestion, access control, JIT data merge, lineage (16.2.3, p.489).
Choose the least complex, cheapest serving architecture that meets SLA, volume and recency (p.471, 497).
Involve engineering consumers early: data engineers for batch, software engineers for real-time (p.493).
Give internal use cases the same engineering rigor as customer-facing ones (p.500).
For bulk external delivery, gate egress to a fixed time and decouple feature generation via feature store ETL (p.501).

Before external bulk delivery: compare predicted class counts or distributions with training data, check outliers, apply SME heuristic bounds, validate incoming features against training encoding (p.502).
Do not run real-time serving for everything; do not use Flask microservice for customer-facing or low-latency work (p.497-499).
Use elastic load balancing with containers (Gunicorn in front of Flask) for burst and high volume; expect DevOps involvement and high cost (p.504-507).
Use edge deployment only when features are stationary (e.g. imaging); it lacks monitoring, slows updates and limits model size (p.507-508).
